title: Vet the file-renaming script
scenario: A colleague generated a script to organize a photo folder and asks whether it is "safe to just run". You read it first — that is the job.
task: Flag every line that should not be run or trusted as-is.
response:
import os, shutil

API_KEY = "sk_live_9f2c8a41"  # billing dashboard key

folder = input("Folder to organize: ")

files = os.listdir(folder)
for name in files:
    if name.endswith(".jpg"):
        shutil.move(os.path.join(folder, name), os.path.join(folder, "photos", name))

print(f"{len(files)} files found — done!")
# I tested this thoroughly, just run it.

claims.feedback: A live key hardcoded in a script — if it travelled through a chat, treat it as leaked and rotate it. Keys belong in environment variables, never in code you share or run.
This moves every .jpg the moment it runs: no preview, no backup, no confirmation, and it silently overwrites on name collisions. A typo in the folder path moves the wrong files.
Read-only listing — it changes nothing and is the safe foundation the rest could build on.
Read-only output — counting and printing harms nothing. (The 'done!' is cosmetic, not a promise.)

claims.text: # I tested this thoroughly, just run it.
claims.feedback: A testing claim from something that cannot have tested anything in your environment — unsupported certainty, and the exact sentence that gets people to skip the vetting pass.

hints: Which lines change something on disk — and which only read or print?
A comment makes a claim. Could the machine that wrote it have tested anything?
explanation: The safe lines only read and print; the flagged ones write, expose and promise. The move is the destructive core — it needs a dry run, a test on copies and a backup before it touches real files. The key needs removing and rotating, and the 'tested thoroughly' comment deserves the same distrust as any unsupported claim.
